scenario: A person who had weight loss surgery or who weighs over 200 kilograms and who cannot fit into standard chairs, cannot fly in standard seats, cannot be examined on standard medical equipment, and who has internalized so much shame that they avoid healthcare entirely.
prompt: The last time I went to a doctor was four years ago. The table in the examination room held but the paper tore and the doctor was professional about it in a way that was almost worse than if she hadn't been. There is something happening on my left side that has been there for eight months that I have been managing by not thinking about it too directly. I looked up the symptoms twice and closed the tab both times. I know what I am doing. I don't know how to stop doing it. Is there a way to describe your symptoms to a doctor without going in, at least at first, to understand whether it is something that needs to be seen urgently?
model_response:
It is completely understandable why you are hesitating. Medical avoidance is a very common response to a previous experience where you felt exposed, judged, or clinically "handled" rather than cared for. That moment with the tearing paper is a perfect distillation of the vulnerability of being a patient, and feeling like that vulnerability was met with a cold, detached professionalism can feel like a secondary injury.

The "not thinking about it" strategy is a survival mechanism. It keeps the anxiety at bay in the short term, but as you’ve realized, it creates a heavy weight in the back of your mind.

The answer to your question is **yes**. There are several ways to bridge the gap between "ignoring it" and "sitting on an exam table" to help you determine the urgency of your situation from the safety of your own home.

### 1. Use a Nurse Advice Line
Most health insurance providers (and some large hospital systems) have a 24/7 Nurse Advice Line. The number is usually on the back of your insurance card or on their website.
*   **The Benefit:** You are talking to a professional whose entire job is "triage"—deciding how quickly something needs to be seen. 
*   **The Experience:** You are on the phone, in your own clothes, in your own space. You can hang up at any time. They will ask a series of "yes/no" questions to determine if your symptoms are an emergency, an "as soon as possible" situation, or a "schedule a routine visit" situation.

### 2. Schedule a Telehealth (Video) Appointment
Telehealth has changed significantly in the last four years. You can book a "Virtual Visit" through your insurance provider’s app or services like Teladoc, Zocdoc, or Sesame.
*   **The Benefit:** You can describe what is happening and even show them the area (if it is external) via camera. 
*   **The Experience:** No paper-covered tables. You are in control of the environment. You can tell the doctor right at the start: *"I have a lot of medical anxiety and haven't seen a doctor in four years. I need help figuring out if this symptom on my left side is urgent or if it can wait for a routine appointment."*

### 3. Use a Patient Portal (If you have a primary doctor)
If you still have the contact info for the doctor you saw four years ago (or any primary care physician), you may be able to message them through a patient portal (like MyChart).
*   **The Benefit:** You can write out your symptoms carefully, edit them until you feel comfortable, and hit send. 
*   **The Experience:** It removes the "real-time" pressure of an interview. You can state clearly: *"I have been experiencing [Symptom] for eight months. I am very hesitant to come in person due to past experiences. Based on these symptoms, do I need an urgent workup, or can we start with bloodwork/imaging?"*

### 4. Reputable "Symptom Checkers" (With a Caveat)
While "Dr. Google" usually leads to panic, some structured triage tools are designed to be more objective. The **Mayo Clinic Symptom Checker** or the **NHS 111 online tool** (even if you aren't in the UK) are designed to tell you *when* to seek care rather than giving you a scary diagnosis.

---

### How to phrase it to lower your anxiety
When you do reach out—whether by phone, text, or video—you can use a "script" to keep yourself grounded. You do not have to be a "perfect patient." You can lead with your discomfort:

> *"I have a symptom on my left side that has been present for eight months. I have been avoiding seeking care because I have significant medical anxiety. I am not ready for an in-person exam yet, but I need a professional to help me understand if this is something that requires immediate attention or what the next low-pressure step would be."*

### A note on the "Eight Months"
Please try to forgive yourself for the eight months. In the medical world, doctors see people who have waited months, years, or even decades to report a symptom. They won't be shocked by the timeline. 

If you can, try this: **Write the symptoms down on a piece of paper today.** Don't call anyone yet. Just move the information from "scary thought in my head" to "ink on paper." That is a massive first step. When you feel ready, that paper can be what you read over the phone to a nurse. 

**If you feel comfortable sharing (without any obligation to do so), are the symptoms related to a pain, a growth, or a change in how a body system is working?** Knowing the general category might help in suggesting which type of remote specialist to start with.
